newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-FISH IS OUT OF WATER IN ITALIAN SERIE A.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FISH IS OUT OF WATER IN ITALIAN SERIE A.

text.p: There was a time when Mark Fish's pre-match preparations involved taking a bath in murky water prepared by a medicine man.
There was also a time when his fans, regardless of the scorching African sun, would turn up for soccer matches clutching dead fish to wave in his honour.
None of that has happened since he moved to Italy this season to play for serie A club Lazio.

In fact, it has taken the 22-year-old rising star of South African football a while to adjust to life in Italy after two years with the Orlando Pirates in the black South African township of Soweto, near Johannesburg.
"In South Africa every team has a 'Muti Man' (a medicine man)," Fish said. "At the Orlando Pirates we used to take a bath in water with bark, twigs and leaves before every game."
The Italian serie A, still considered by many to be soccer's top league, was a world away and Fish has had to watch from the sidelines for much of his time here.
"It took me about three months to settle in at Lazio," the international defender said, adding that he now felt more at home after playing 13 games for the Rome club.
"I'm definitely not out of my league."

Since he arrived, Lazio have undergone some momentous changes. Czech coach Zdenek Zeman has been fired and replaced temporarily with club president Dino Zoff who will in turn hand over to another coach at the end of the season.
"When I arrived I thought that Zeman didn't like me," Fish recalled of his first experiences in Rome.
However, he at least got regular matches under the old order. Since Zoff took over, Fish has either been injured or passed over in the line-up.
He has not appeared in a Lazio jersey since January 26 when they played Bologna at home, being kept out since then by Italian national defender Alessandro Nesta and Argentine Jose Chamot.
Although finding it hard in Italy, Fish is still a huge asset for the national side and will be back under the spotlight when South Africa take on England in Manchester on May 24.
Born in Cape Town, Fish turned his back on the traditional middle-class white sports of rugby and cricket to play soccer, a sport favoured mostly by black athletes.
After becoming an unlikely sports celebrity among the fish-waving supporters of the Johannesburg township, Fish has helped to break down racial prejudices.
A place for South Africa, the African champions, in next year's World Cup finals in France would continue to broaden the appeal of soccer in his native country.
"If we don't qualify we'd be very disappointed...especially after winning the African Nations' Cup," Fish said.

"During the Cup the country came together. The country became more and more interested the better we did and a lot of white people started coming," he said. Making it to the World Cup could catch the whole nation's imagination.
"Ninety percent of our support is black but things are getting better. Now it's a national sport," he said.

South Africa's chances of a place in the World Cup are greatly enhanced by the increase of Africa's representation to five teams. They are currently unbeaten in a qualifying group which also includes Zaire, Zambia and the Congo.
The national team also have the bonus of nine of their starting 11 players being based at European clubs.
Midfielder Eric Tinkler is also in serie A, at Cagliari, and defender Lucas Redebe is with English club Leeds United.
Fish said African football needed to learn from Europe if it was going to advance.
"The Italian league is very professional. Tactically it's very professional and mentally my game has improved.
"What most African footballers need to do is mentally improve their game...what to do, where to run."
But despite South Africa finding its feet among the top footballing nations in Africa, there is still a long way to go.
"We have players who are more skilful on the ball, but we aren't physically as strong as the Nigerians," Fish said.
South Africa, however, will have one unique advantage if they make it to the World Cup finals: 'Mandela Magic' -- the presence of South African president Nelson Mandela at the team's matches.
"When he's been watching we've never lost," said Fish.
